cards.explanation: The astrologers ask the king to tell them the dream. They answer the king in Aramaic with this: "O king, may you live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation." Sounds polite, right? They're asking for the one thing they need to start. It's like a mechanic saying, "Just tell me what the noise sounds like," except the noise is inside the king's head.

The king demands both the dream and its interpretation. He says, "If you do not tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will be cut into pieces and your houses will be reduced to rubble." Read that again, friends. He wants them to say what he dreamed AND what it means. That's like your boss saying, "Write the email I'm thinking of, then answer it."

The word is "stalling." The king says, "I know for sure that you are stalling for time because you see that my word is final." He has heard this request twice now, and he's done. I've stalled on a few things in my day myself. A king who's already decided is the worst person to try it on.

The answer is False. The king does not say the wise men have been honest. He says, "You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change." Those are strong words, friends. He wants the dream told so he will know they can give him its interpretation.

The answer is True. The astrologers say, "What the king requests is so difficult that no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals." They're telling the king this is beyond any person. Keep that line in your pocket, friends, because Daniel is about to answer it.

The answer is Daniel and his friends. The decree says the wise men are to be executed, and men go looking for Daniel and his friends to execute them. Daniel is one of the king's wise men, and his friends are Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah (Daniel 2:17). The order doesn't skip anybody. I think that's a heavy moment for these four.

Daniel asks Arioch why the king's decree is so harsh. His words are, "Why is the decree from the king so harsh?" The text says that when Arioch, the commander of the king's guard, went out to execute the wise men, Daniel responded with discretion and tact. A question, not a speech. Then Arioch explained the situation to him.

The word is "time." Daniel goes in and asks the king to give him some time, so that he could give him the interpretation. The astrologers asked for the dream, but Daniel asks for time. A man walking in to ask a favor of the king who just ordered the execution takes nerve. I'd have sent a card.

The word is "mercy." Daniel urges his friends to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that he and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Four men, one prayer request. When the problem is bigger than you, friends, you go to the One who isn't.

Daniel blesses the God of heaven. The text says that during the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven. His response is praise, not a victory lap. Then he declares the praise out loud, and we get to hear it in the next verses.

The answer is True. Daniel says of God, "He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them." Hold on to that, friends. He's saying it about a king who can order the whole wise-men crew executed, and Daniel says the God of heaven is the One who sets kings up.

The answer is False. Daniel says, "He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him." God does know what lies in darkness. That's exactly why He could reveal a dream that nobody in the room could touch.

The word is "execute." Daniel tells Arioch, "Do not execute the wise men of Babylon! Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation." Arioch is the man the king appointed to destroy them, so this is a big ask. Daniel isn't only speaking up for himself here. He's speaking up for the whole group.

The answer is that none of them can explain this mystery. Daniel says, "No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires." The wise men themselves said as much (Daniel 2:10). Daniel doesn't take the credit, friends. He's about to point somewhere else.

God has made known what will happen in the future. Daniel says God "…has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days." He calls God "…the Revealer of Mysteries…" in the next verse. The king lay on his bed thinking about the future, and God showed him what's ahead.

The answer is False. Daniel says the mystery was revealed "…not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your mind." Daniel keeps the spotlight off himself. It's a humble thing to say to a king.

The feet are part iron and part clay. Daniel says its legs were iron, and "…its feet were part iron and part clay." Strong metal on top, and something that crumbles at the very bottom. Remember that, friends, because the stone goes right for those feet.
The answer is True. Daniel says the stone "…struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them." The stone was cut out, but not by human hands. The feet are where it lands.

The word is "mountain." Daniel says, "…the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth." A stone that ends up filling the whole earth. The statue got shattered and blown away, and the stone became a mountain.
The king is the head of gold. Daniel tells the king, "You are that head of gold." The king gets the top spot and the best metal. I'd have taken that spot too, no question.

The fourth kingdom will shatter and crush all the others. Daniel says, "for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others." The picture is iron doing what iron does. This fourth kingdom does that to all the others.

The answer is False. Daniel calls it "…a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it." So it has strength, but it's split. The peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together.

The answer is False. Daniel says the God of heaven will set up a kingdom "…that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people." It's the one kingdom in this whole story that never gets passed along. It "…will itself stand forever."

The king falls on his face. The text says King Nebuchadnezzar "…fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel…" This is the king who ordered the wise men destroyed. Now he's on the floor. I think that's a moment he did not see coming.

The answer is True. The king says, "Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery." A king says that about somebody else's God. Big words from a man who had become so angry and furious earlier in this chapter (Daniel 2:12).

The answer is Babylon. The king made Daniel "…ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." That's a long way from the decree that sent men to look for Daniel and his friends to execute them. Daniel ends the chapter with a big job.

The answer is True. The king made Daniel "…ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." That's the same group that was almost executed. Daniel went from being counted among them to being in charge of them.

The king appoints Daniel's three friends. At Daniel's request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon. Those are the names given to Daniel's friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (Daniel 1:6, 7). They're the three he urged to plead for mercy from the God of heaven. Daniel remained in the king's court.
